key_insight: This audit found no racial or sex differences surviving study-wide correction, while pain-management recommendations varied substantially across models and settings.
clinical_relevance: Clinical AI fairness evaluations should test each deployed configuration, because model and setting choices may affect recommendations more than patient identity in these tasks.
method: Study 1 tested four open-weight models on six acute-pain vignettes, varying race and sex through explicit labels or names.
Identity comparisons were paired to a White male reference using the same case and sampling seed.
Study 2 evaluated 24 configurations of 17 models on the same vignettes and 50 clinician-written Q-Pain cases.
evidence_signal: None of 1,386 Study 2 comparisons survived false-discovery-rate correction; all pain-severity differences met equivalence bounds of ±1 point on a 0–10 scale.
watch_item: These exploratory, single-prompt findings do not establish absence of bias: opioid estimates were less precise, with Study 1 unable to exclude differences of about 20 percentage points.
paper_title: Do Large Language Models Show Racial and Sex Bias in Pain Management? A Counterfactual Audit of GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, DeepSeek and Qwen
